title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 237
paragraphs: The third of the explanations is much the most plausible, but nevertheless the most mistaken of all; for this one has no more truth in it than the others, alleging as it does that the Nile flows from melting snow — whereas in fact it flows out of Libya through the midst of the Ethiopians, and so comes out into Egypt. How then should it flow from snow, when it flows from the hottest parts to those which are cooler? Indeed most of the facts are such as to convince any reasoning man that it is not at all likely it flows from snow. The first and greatest evidence is the winds, which blow hot from these regions; the second is that the land there is always rainless and without frost, whereas after snow has fallen rain must necessarily come within five days, so that if it snowed in those parts rain would fall there; the third evidence is the people dwelling there, who are black in colour because of the burning heat. Moreover, kites and swallows remain there throughout the year and do not leave the land; and cranes, fleeing the cold that sets in over Scythia, come regularly to these parts to winter. If then it snowed ever so little in the land through which the Nile flows and in which it has its rise, none of these things could take place, as necessity compels us to admit.
